candidate.architecture_role: single C++/ggml/GGUF speech-engine challenger for the already admitted Qwen3-ASR family

source_observations.finding: CrispASR presents a single C++ binary with multiple ASR/TTS backends, includes a Qwen3 backend, GGUF loading and auto-download support; this is source capability only and not Frankenstein runtime evidence.

The Qwen3 CLI adapter implements a full transcription path around mel extraction, encoder execution, ChatML/audio-token injection, KV prefill and greedy/beam decoding, so the source surface is materially beyond the stale Stage-1 file-header comment in src/qwen3_asr.cpp.

The generated CrispASR feature matrix does not declare the qwen3 or qwen3-1.7b backend with the Streaming capability bit, while nemotron is explicitly marked Streaming. Therefore native/stateful Qwen3-ASR streaming must not be claimed from source.

CrispASR's generic --stream/--mic/--live front-end is documented to work with every supported backend by sliding-window chunking. Default pipe streaming uses a 10 s rolling window with a 3 s step; structured finalization can re-decode buffered utterance PCM. This can provide realtime wrapper behavior without proving backend-native streaming.

The structured streaming path supports explicit partial/final/silence events and final-on-silence timing; redecode is the default finalization mode and adds an extra backend pass, creating a latency/compute tradeoff that must be measured on clay-direct-dev.

Strict-pipeline logic exists for explicitly requested VAD, word-timestamp and punctuation stages: default behavior may degrade gracefully when a stage fails, while strict mode turns requested-stage failure into an error. Trigger-7 evidence runs should use explicit strict requirements for any post-processing stage that is part of acceptance.

src/qwen3_asr.cpp retains a top-of-file comment describing only a Stage-1 conv-front-end implementation even though the current adapter invokes encoder and LLM/KV functions. This is a documentation/source-coherence warning, not proof that the runtime is incomplete; exact executable target tests outrank the stale comment.

positive: CrispASR is worth retaining as a low-integration-cost C++/GGUF Qwen3-ASR challenger because one binary can expose file, live, JSON-stream and server surfaces.
Its generic streaming wrapper provides a concrete path to partial/final utterance events without requiring a Python model stack.
The explicit strict-stage controls are useful for fail-closed benchmark receipts.
negative_or_unproven: Qwen3-ASR native/stateful streaming is not source-proven and is explicitly absent from the current backend capability matrix.
German WER, German code-switch accuracy, TTFA, p95/p99 latency, RSS, sustained realtime factor, cancellation behavior and long-session stability are unobserved on Frankenstein hardware.
Generic sliding-window streaming may repeatedly decode overlapping context and the default redecode finalization adds work; source presence alone cannot establish a low-latency Pareto win.
Auto-download is convenient but must not be used as provenance for an evidence-bearing target run; model/runtime artifacts need exact revision/hash pins before execution.

hypothesis: On the measured clay-direct-dev resource envelope, CrispASR plus a pinned Qwen3-ASR GGUF may reduce integration complexity and still achieve acceptable German partial/final responsiveness despite lacking backend-native streaming.
counterhypothesis: The chunked/redecode wrapper cost makes Qwen3-ASR too slow or jittery for conversational Trigger-7 targets, while a backend with declared native streaming such as the already-pinned Nemotron streaming candidate wins latency and stability; CrispASR/Qwen3 then remains useful only for offline/final-quality ASR.
